title: Descartes and the rationalists
note: Rationalists held that reason, not the senses alone, is the main source of knowledge, and that some ideas are innate. Descartes doubted everything he could, found his own thinking existence certain, and rebuilt knowledge on God's existence and clear and distinct ideas. Spinoza and Leibniz built rival systems on similar principles.

read.title: Doubt as a road to certainty
text: René Descartes wanted knowledge as secure as geometry. In the Meditations he resolved to set aside any belief he could find the least reason to doubt. The senses sometimes deceive, and he could not be sure he was not dreaming. He even imagined a powerful deceiver bent on fooling him about everything.

Yet one thing survived. However much he was deceived, he had to exist in order to be deceived. 'I am, I exist' is certain whenever he thinks it. He then asked what he was, and answered: a thinking thing, one that doubts, understands, wills, and imagines.

From this foundation Descartes argued that he has an idea of an infinite, perfect being, and that a finite mind could not produce such an idea by itself, so God exists. A perfect God would not deceive, so whatever we perceive clearly and distinctly is true. On that basis he restored knowledge of the physical world and concluded that mind, whose nature is thought, is distinct from body, whose nature is extension.
Critics pressed him. Arnauld asked whether the argument runs in a circle, and Princess Elisabeth asked how an unextended mind could move an extended body.
